pg:https://www.wired.com/story/chinas-nv.desc: China’s use of sexpionage is a well-established intelligence tactic with recent, high-profile examples. So how did the world’s most powerful AI executive fall for it?
paras: Jensen Huang surely doesn’t live a typical life—he’s a centibillionaire, the swashbuckling CEO of Nvidia, one of the hottest and most geopolitically consequential companies of the 21st century. In fact, it’s hard to think of many companies in the world that would be a higher priority target for foreign intelligence agencies.

All of that makes the stock-shaking news this week all the more surprising. How did Huang get embroiled in a spy scandal that mixes infidelity, international espionage, the Trump administration, and the economic behemoth of the multitrillion-dollar AI industry?

The story kicked off just before Halloween, with a six-byline story in The New York Times reporting that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot. Starting somewhere between 2024 and 2025, Huang allegedly had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a one-time executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider known as Megaspeed. US intelligence agencies warned top US officials that they believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset. So far, Nvidia’s board, which has launched its own investigation, says it has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” but that’s far from the only concern.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/books/202.desc: Kazuo Ishiguro, Jeff VanderMeer, Olivia Laing and other writers weigh in on the publishing world’s genre wars
paras: Ella CreamerWed 11 Nov 2026 16.44 GMTLast modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 18.42 GMTShare Prefer the Guardian on Google As M John Harrison was announced as the Booker prize winner on Monday evening, the 81-year-old looked gobsmacked. Decades into his career, and long overlooked by the mainstream literary establishment, he had just won a prize that has never before rewarded a writer known for science fiction, with a decidedly fantastical book.

His fans, many leading authors among them, are thrilled. “For decades it was a standard – and correct – nerd whine to point out that sentence for sentence, book for book, Harrison was one of the greatest writers out there, full stop, but that ‘mainstream’ prizes never reflected that,” says China Miéville, who last week won the Goldsmiths prize with his 1,200-page speculative novel The Rouse. Back in 2002, Miéville wrote that Harrison not having won a Booker by that point proved “the bankruptcy and back-slapping generic snobbery of the literary establishment”. Now, he says: “I am so delighted, for Harrison, and for fiction.”

While some past Booker-winning authors draw heavily on SF – Margaret Atwood, Kazuo Ishiguro, Ian McEwan – Harrison is the first winner from the “bona fide SF” sphere, said Booker prize foundation chief executive Gaby Wood on Monday. The Pulitzer and the Nobel rarely take notice of SF either, though the latter has honoured Ishiguro and Doris Lessing – both of whom are considered literary writers who dabble in SF, rather than purists, and thus perhaps considered more palatable to a wider reading public.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/games/202.desc: The developers behind its virtual Florida share how they built their most ambitious world so far
paras: Keza MacDonaldWed 11 Nov 2026 15.00 GMTLast modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 17.49 GMTShare Prefer the Guardian on Google In 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North took their first trips to Miami to do field research for the next game in the phenomenally popular crime series. “Before you’re doing hyper-organised research trips, you’re immersing yourself in the place and its history, the vibe of it,” Rob Nelson, one of the lead developers on GTA VI, tells me. “[You see] the physical places you want to move characters through, the experiences you want them to have, and the juxtaposition between the extremes of society that are in Miami.”

I wondered: did people ever recognise them on any of their research trips? Did locals know what they were doing? This is the biggest game in the world, after all; I imagine it would be difficult to go entirely undercover. “We’re always semi-undercover,” he says. “But if you have a bunch of dorks going through a terrifying neighbourhood, you do stick out a bit.”

paras: A powerful new computer simulation is allowing scientists to explore one of the most mysterious periods in cosmic history, when the universe emerged from darkness and the first stars and galaxies began to transform the cosmos.

Developed by researchers at MIT, Harvard University, and other institutions, the simulation, called Lumina, recreates the evolution of the early universe across a region roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide. It follows 2 billion years of cosmic history, revealing how galaxies formed, how radiation spread through space, and how the universe gradually became transparent to light.

The research, published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), provides an unusually detailed picture of events that unfolded billions of years before our solar system existed.

The new simulation, called Lumina, re-creates how the first stars and black holes drove reionization, a pivotal but enigmatic phase that transformed the universe. Following the big bang, ultraviolet radiation from these early light sources stripped electrons from hydrogen atoms, the most common element in space, allowing light to travel farther and changing how galaxies formed.

The early universe has become an exciting new frontier for astronomers seeking to understand how the cosmos evolved into what it is today. Because light takes time to travel through space, powerful telescopes capture distant galaxies as they appeared billions of years ago. But studying such a long stretch of cosmic history requires simulations on a similarly vast scale. That's where models such as Lumina come in.

paras: The light will continue its journey while you sleep, while you eat, while you go to work. Only when you reach the same time tomorrow could its photons potentially wash over a spacecraft more than 16 billion miles away.

That robotic probe is NASA's Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object in the universe. It will cross the one light-day-away milestone at 5:16 a.m. ET on Wednesday, Nov. 18. One light-day is the distance light travels over 24 hours. Radio signals move at the speed of light, so any message from Earth would need a full day to reach the spacecraft. Considering Voyager 1 never stops moving, that communication lag will only increase.

To mark the occasion, the U.S. space agency has a couple of things planned, one of which involves pointing that flashlight toward the sky. The day after the milestone, you can watch the mission team talk about where the spacecraft has been and how it keeps going.

paras: Peter BradshawThu 12 Nov 2026 17.14 GMTFirst published on Thu 12 Nov 2026 09.00 GMTShare Prefer the Guardian on Google Here for lovers of Dickens – and fans of subtext – is an unexpectedly watchable new movie version of A Christmas Carol starring a top-hatted and heavily madeup Johnny Depp; it is a film about whether it’s possible for a man to earn redemption before it is too late. (The answer is … sure, as long as you say sorry and change your ways. But Mr Scrooge never launched a libel action against the Sun for calling him an un-Christmassy old meanie.)

There is a witty and ingenious new prologue sequence in which Scrooge’s equally grumpy partner Jacob Marley, played by Ian McKellen, is still alive, going into a full Stadler-and-Waldorf double-act with his old colleague. (Wait – did The Muppet Christmas Carol inspire this?) And West shows us his scary-movie style by having that scene coming to a disturbing close with a kettle’s eerie whistle as it comes to the boil.

As well as pointedly asking about prisons and workhouses, Scrooge now actually accuses the charitable gentlemen of stealing the donations themselves, and there’s a terrible new end in store for cheerful Mr Fezziwig, which the film suggests is what finally embittered Scrooge against the undeserving poor. His lost love Belle is here a novelist, an idea borrowed from romance author Michelle Griep. Andrea Riseborough, Tramell Tillman and Robert Strange play the three ghosts; Rupert Grint is his pinch-faced clerk Bob Cratchit, and Sam Claflin is his cheerful nephew Fred, son of his once adored sister Fanny.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/football/.desc: The captain’s penalty on the night he earned his 126th cap gave England a 2-1 Nations League victory against Croatia and progress to the Nations League quarter-finals
paras: England had demolished Croatia 7-0 in Rijeka last month; it was Croatia’s heaviest defeat. It was a different story here. England lacked cut and thrust. There was a flatness to the Wembley atmosphere. Croatia were never likely to be humbled again and they sensed redemption when Petar Sucic capitalised upon a defensive aberration from Jarell Quansah to equalise for 1-1 just before the hour.

It was over to Kane from the spot. There was the familiar stutter and the conversion was clipped up the middle, narrowly avoiding the trailing leg of the goalkeeper, Dominik Livakovic. It was Kane’s 92nd England goal; his 27th successful penalty.

Croatia fought until the end and they had a clutch of late chances, none better than when Nikola Vlasic took a touch and shot just wide in the 82nd minute. England were good value for the result. They are guaranteed a place in the quarter-finals of this competition in March and will go to Madrid to play Spain on Sunday with a shot at winning the group. They would have to beat the world champions to do that. And, really, play better than this.

pg:https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/faa-g.desc: U.S. flights are resuming after the FAA ground stop, but delays and cancellations are still piling up.
paras: U.S. flights resumed Saturday after the Federal Aviation Administration halted flight departures across the country for more than four hours on Friday, leading to thousands of flight delays and cancellations.

There were more than 6,200 delays and more than 3,400 cancellations as of early Saturday, according to FlightAware.

More than 6,600 flights were cancelled and 8,600 delayed, with another 1,500 already cancelled for Sunday, according to FlightRadar24. Aviation analysts said the four-hour nationwide grounding could disrupt airline ⁠schedules for days. It was the longest flight shutdown since the attacks of September 11 2001.

The FAA lifted the ground stop later on Friday, with transportation secretary Sean Duffy saying US airspace reopened at 8.15pm ET (0115 GMT). But departures would ⁠resume gradually and it would take ​time for airlines to restore normal operations, he warned. “It’s going to be slow.”
